There are many more than four cases in the language (bordering on 15, and still growing), but these are the ones that are the most important. I'm not quite sure what to call these cases, linguistically, because the actual, linguistic case that they represent changes depending on verbs and conjugations. Even so, in the language itself, they're called active, passive, and receiving.

Starting with the easiest, the receiving is just that. It's the noun in the sentence that receives something. This also includes it having something, in the case of dayaude (to have). In the case of tsal, to make, it is what is being made. In this way, it can either be nominative (I have, I receive) or accusative (I make it), and sometimes dative (I give it to you). This case will usually be the last noun phrase in the sentence, only separable affixes coming after it, and is marked with the article dee /nɛ/ (pronouns change form depending on case, and don't require articles to preface them, unless it's a minor case)

Next up is active. Active can be nominative or accusative, depending on the verb and if it's conjugated. We'll get to the conjugations after we're done with the cases; first, lets see when it's in which case. For teiab, to give, and tsal, to make, it will be nominative. For baud, to receive, and for dayaude, to have, it will be accusative. This case will be the first noun phrase, unless you're specifying a conjunction. This case is marked with the article je /ʒɛ/.

Finally, the passive case, marked with the article tuu /tu/, which is only used with one verb, or in specific forms of other verbs (such as imperative, where pretty much all the cases get rearranged). This case is used with teiab, to give, and is accusative. It simply doesn't exist, for the other verbs. It comes after the active case, and before all minor cases.

With all of this said, here's some examples:

I make an apple
Make I the apple
Tsal e dee Eidal
/tsal ɛ nɛ ʔedal/

I give you an apple
Give I the apple you
Teiab e tuu Eidal aude
/teab ɛ tu edal on/

You receive an apple
Receive the apple you
Baud je Eidal aude
/bod ʒɛ ʔedal on/

You have an apple
Have the apple you
Dayaude je Eidal aude
/dajon ʒɛ ʔedal on/

Okay, now, I'll explain how these change when the verb is conjugated. You always conjugate for the nominative, no matter what case it's in. This means that the some cases will disappear, and others will be replaced by nouns in other cases.

With tsal, the active case is nominative. This is simply removed, and only the receiving case and minor cases are left.

With teiab, the active is nominative. Whatever noun was in that case is taken out, and the noun from the passive case is put into the active case.

With baud, the receiving case is nominative. This is simply removed. Same with dayaude.

Now, if we conjugate the previous examples, we're left with this:

Tsal'de dee Eidal
/tsalɛdɛ nɛ ʔedal/

Teiab'de je Eidal aude
/teabɛdɛ ʒɛ ʔedal on/

Baud'dau je Eidal
/bodɛdo ʒɛ ʔedal/

Dayaude'dau je Eidal
/dayonɛdo ʒɛ ʔedal/

That pretty much wraps it up, folks.

That's interesting. What are the differences, if any, between snetences with conjugated verbs and ones with unconjugated verbs?

Aside from the cases, you can't attach an affix to a conjugated verb, with the exception of the negating "kú.". They have to be separated, and put at the end of the sentence. Of course, you could do it, but it would be grammatically incorrect, just like if you attached one to a verb in the infinitive. Conjugating also opens up the use of another case, which isn't used if the verb is unconjugated. This case is used to refer back to the conjugation, when you want to specify what you're talking about. It's basically a glorified nominative. For example, if I were to say "She gave me an apple," I could translate it as "Teiab'da je Eidal ede taulaú," or, if I wanted to specifically say that it was a girl who gave me an apple (the third person is gender neutral), I could say "Teiab'da kau Giiaú'eke je Eidal ede taulaú," which means "The girl gave me an apple." If I were to not conjugate the verb, I could say "Taulaú'teiab a tuu Eidal ede," or "Taulaú'teiab je Giiaú'eke tuu Eidal ede," respectively.
